result: The study generated a large-scale MCFO image resource from 5155 Gen1 GAL4 lines, comprising 74,337 fly samples with an average of 14 brain and 7 VNC images per line. Two collections were created: a 20×/63× collection (2463 lines, 27,546 samples, 94.2% female, focused on brain and optic lobes) and a 40× collection (4575 lines, 46,791 samples, 44.9% female, covering central brain and VNC but excluding optic lobes).
evaluation: Claims C33-C62 provide comprehensive documentation of the dataset scope, composition, and design rationale. The quantitative metrics (number of lines, samples, sex distribution) are clearly stated and internally consistent across claims. The exclusion of optic lobes from the 40× collection is justified by existing resources (C60-C61), though neurons connecting optic lobes to central brain remain identifiable (C62).

result: Phase 1 used R57C10-Flp on 4562 GAL4 lines generating 27,226 brains and 26,512 VNCs. Lines were categorized by expression density (Categories 1-5), with 95% falling in the desired range (Categories 2-4). Phase 2 optimized parameters by switching to hs-Flp, focusing on Category 2-3 lines, adjusting heat shock duration (40 min for Category 2, 13 min for Category 3), and prioritizing brain over VNC imaging based on neuron count differences.
evaluation: Claims C63-C87 and C233-C235 describe a systematic two-phase approach with clear optimization rationale. The categorization system (C69-C75) provides a qualitative framework for line selection. The switch from R57C10-Flp to hs-Flp (C80-C82) and heat shock optimization (C83-C86) are justified by prior work (C83-C84). The brain/VNC prioritization (C234-C235) is supported by neuron count estimates, though the estimates vary widely (37-100k vs 15-20k).

result: MCFO labeling density was optimized to balance neuron identifiability: too sparse yields few neurons, too dense causes overlap. Density control was achieved by adjusting Flp activity through driver selection or heat shock duration. The 20×/63× collection customized density for specific CNS regions, while the 40× collection standardized then optimized based on GAL4 expression density. Many lines lack a globally ideal Flp level due to regional expression heterogeneity.
evaluation: Claims C52-C57 describe the technical challenge and solution for optimizing MCFO labeling. The approach is logical and supported by citation (C53). The acknowledgment that no single Flp level is ideal for all regions (C57) demonstrates methodological sophistication. However, the claims lack quantitative metrics for what constitutes 'optimal' density.

result: R57C10-Flp and hs-Flp showed differential labeling patterns. R57C10-Flp is thought to label only postmitotic neurons, while hs-Flp labels most cell types including glia (8% of Phase 2 lines). Kenyon cells were labeled at different rates: hs-Flp MCFO (93%), UAS-GFP (24%), and R57C10-Flp MCFO (10%) in a 460-line sample. Most lines (55%) showed unlabeled Kenyon cells with GFP and R57C10-Flp but labeled with hs-Flp.
evaluation: Claims C213-C224 document systematic differences between Flp drivers based on a 10% sample (460 lines). The quantitative results (C216, C221-C223) are specific and internally consistent. The differential Kenyon cell labeling is well-documented, though the underlying mechanism is not explained. The observation that glial labeling doesn't impair 3D visualization (C217) is useful but qualitative.

result: A characteristic ascending neuron ('sparse T') with cell body near the metathoracic ganglion and T-shaped projections was observed at very high frequency: >60% of lines with MCFO reporters (67/107 in Phase 1, 64/107 in Phase 2) and 22/107 lines with UAS-GFP. This high frequency is attributed to properties of the GAL4 collections rather than sampling artifacts. No other neuron was as frequently labeled.
evaluation: Claims C225-C230 document an unexpected finding with clear quantitative support from a 107-line sample. The comparison across reporters (MCFO vs GFP) strengthens the inference that this reflects GAL4 collection properties (C229). However, the sample size is relatively small (107 lines = 2% of total), and the biological significance of this observation is unclear.

result: NeuronBridge was developed as a publicly available search tool implementing two complementary approaches: CDM (comparing color depth MIPs without full skeletonization) and PPPM (using NBLAST-derived scores to find optimal neuron segment combinations). The tool provides pre-computed searches across published datasets and custom search capability with cloud-based processing (~3000 threads, completing in minutes). All data were registered to JRC2018 templates.
evaluation: Claims C96-C119 describe a comprehensive computational resource with clear technical specifications. The two search approaches (CDM and PPPM) are well-documented with citations (C99-C110). The custom search capability (C116-C119) demonstrates practical utility. However, the claims are primarily descriptive of tool functionality rather than validation of search performance.

result: Forward analysis of 10 Hemibrain bodies showed both CDM and PPPM identified many correct matches in the top 100 results. CDM identified 17.6±8.3 correct lines per body, PPPM identified 20.1±10.6. Performance varied by neuron (LC18: PPPM 24 vs CDM 13; CT1: CDM 8 vs PPPM 3). Each approach uniquely identified lines not found by the other (CDM: 8.2±6.1, PPPM: 10.7±8.7). All 10 neurons yielded ≥9 matching lines, though this may not generalize to all neurons.
evaluation: Claims C120-C141 provide quantitative evaluation of search performance with appropriate statistical reporting (means and standard deviations). The complementarity of CDM and PPPM is well-demonstrated (C133-C135). However, the evaluation is limited to 10 neurons selected by anatomical experts (C121), which may introduce selection bias. The acknowledgment that results may not generalize (C140) and that expansion could improve coverage (C141) appropriately qualifies the findings.

result: Reverse analysis examined 9 Hemibrain bodies with 2-13 published split-GAL4 associations. Both PPPM and CDM had median line ranks under 100 for most bodies. PPPM was more consistent (33-80% of known matches in top 50) compared to CDM (0-100%). Each approach performed better on some neurons than the other.
evaluation: Claims C142-C146 extend prior PPPM analysis (C142) with CDM comparison. The reverse analysis provides complementary validation using known associations. PPPM's greater consistency (C145) is quantitatively supported, though the wide range for CDM (0-100%) suggests high variability. The sample size (9 bodies) is small but uses published ground truth data.

result: Qualitative observations from practical use indicate: (1) CDM and PPPM are complementary, with PPPM bringing matches closer to top results; (2) CDM struggles with occluded neurons, benefiting from 3D stack examination; (3) PPPM shows most improvement with occluded neurons; (4) both return highly-ranked false positives, making rankings alone insufficient for algorithmic association; (5) the collection and techniques can lead to good split combinations for 50-80% of cell types; (6) more hemidrivers would be needed to increase this rate; (7) techniques simplify candidate identification without requiring extensive anatomical expertise.
evaluation: Claims C147-C154 provide valuable practical insights but are explicitly qualitative observations rather than systematic evaluations. The 50-80% success rate estimate (C152) lacks supporting data or methodology. The observations about false positives (C151) and complementarity (C147-C150) align with quantitative results but are not independently validated. These represent expert opinions rather than rigorously tested conclusions.

result: Several caveats limit split-GAL4 success: (1) many cell types contain morphologically indistinguishable neurons, so matches may label different neurons within a type; (2) split-GAL4 hemidrivers can differ from Gen1 GAL4 in vector sequence and insertion site, altering expression; (3) UAS reporters vary in insertion site and UAS elements, affecting labeling; (4) MCFO reporters may brightly label weakly-labeled neurons; (5) GAL4 expression can vary temporally, causing spatial but not temporal overlap. Examining full Gen1 patterns can help predict split combination effectiveness.
evaluation: Claims C155-C162 provide important limitations and caveats based on established knowledge of the GAL4 system. These are well-reasoned explanations for why EM/LM matches don't always yield successful split-GAL4 lines. The claims appropriately acknowledge biological and technical factors that complicate the matching process. However, no quantitative data is provided on the frequency or impact of these issues.

result: The cellular-resolution image collection enables identification of GAL4 driver lines with expression in single neurons without new experiments, enabling analyses impossible with full GAL4 patterns. Single-cell data are particularly useful for EM/LM matching. LM data complement EM by: (1) providing independent quality checks for EM reconstructions; (2) revealing variable features through multiple cell type examples; (3) providing full cell shapes for neurons only partly in EM volumes (e.g., Hemibrain lacks neurons spanning hemispheres or projecting to/from VNC). Automated approaches are essential for efficient large-scale use.
evaluation: Claims C88-C95 articulate the utility and complementary nature of the resource. The advantages of cellular resolution (C88-C89) and LM/EM integration (C90-C94) are logical and supported by citations (C91). The limitation of the Hemibrain dataset (C94) provides concrete justification for the resource. However, these are primarily inferences about utility rather than demonstrated applications.

result: The study optimized driver line selection, sample preparation, and imaging to maximize identifiable neurons. Two complementary search approaches were implemented in an easy-to-use interface. The resource should be amenable to future search approaches. Beyond the EM-to-split-GAL4 use case, other uses include guiding EM proofreading and extending EM analyses beyond limited regions. NeuronBridge has already seen frequent usage in published studies. The tools enable rapid determination of split-GAL4 lines to target neurons in the Hemibrain and eventually the full CNS.
evaluation: Claims C163-C167, C231-C232 summarize the resource's impact and utility. The frequent usage (C231) is supported by multiple citations. The claim about rapid determination of split-GAL4 lines (C232) is supported by the search evaluation results. However, the claim about 'most neurons' in the Hemibrain is not quantitatively validated—the forward analysis only examined 10 neurons.

result: Detailed methods are provided for fly rearing, crosses, heat shock, dissection, immunohistochemistry (hybrid chemical tag and antibody labeling), imaging (8 Zeiss LSM 710/780 microscopes over 11 years, multiple objectives and resolutions), image processing (automated pipeline using Janelia Workstation), data storage (AWS S3 in H5J format), NeuronBridge implementation (React framework, serverless AWS deployment, burst-parallel computing), quality control, categorization, and search evaluation protocols.
evaluation: Claims C168-C212 provide comprehensive methodological documentation with appropriate technical detail and citations. The methods are reproducible and well-specified. The quality control criteria (C202-C205) are clearly stated. The acknowledgment of potential metadata errors (C205) is appropriately cautious. The categorization approach (C206-C209) is qualitative but clearly described. The search evaluation methods (C210-C212) are adequately specified.
